notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Lamentations 1, compiled from the sources I could access.

---

## Lamentations 1: Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview

The chapter is an acrostic poem: each of the 22 verses begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. **Ellicott** notes the poem divides into two halves: vv. 1–11 where the prophet laments over Jerusalem as an observer, and vv. 12–22 where "the daughter of Zion bewails her own miseries" in first person. **Guzik (Enduring Word)** cites H.L. Ellison that the acrostic symbolizes "the completeness — 'the A to Z' — of grief." **Constable** says Jeremiah's "first dirge established the book's theme — the sorrow of sin."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 1: "How lonely lies the city, once so full of people! She who was great among the nations has become a widow. The princess of the provinces has become a slave."

*   **Gill** says the Hebrew word "How" (*Echah*) expresses astonishment, not an inquiry into causes. The city "sits" — the posture of mourners (cf. Ezra 9:3; Neh 1:4). Jerusalem is "as a widow" because her king (her "head and husband") is taken captive and God has departed. **Gill** cites Jarchi (a medieval Jewish commentator) that it is "as a widow," not "a widow" outright, because her Husband would return. **Gill** also notes that Vespasian struck a coin after conquering Judea showing a woman under a palm tree with the inscription *Judea Capta*, corresponding to this very image. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Ellicott** reads the verse as one sentence: "She is become a widow that was great among the nations." "Provinces" refers to neighbouring countries once subject to Judah (as in the reign of Hezekiah). "Tributary" implies personal servitude rather than mere money payment (see Josh 16:10). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Pulpit Commentary** agrees the verse is three parallel lines. "Widow" is a symbol of desolation and misery — not to be pressed as though God as Husband is directly meant (contra some readings). "Provinces" suggests the writer lived under Babylonian rule, using the administrative language of empire. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/1.htm

*   **Keil & Delitzsch**: "She sits solitary" is intensified by "she has become like a widow." The "princess among the provinces" refers to the flourishing period under David and Solomon when other nations paid tribute to Jerusalem. Now she has become a "soccager" (forced labourer). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/1-1.htm

*   **Clarke (Methodist):** "How doth the city sit solitary" — sitting with the elbow on the knee, head supported by hand, no company — all signs of mourning. The widow imagery reflects loss of her king. The Hindu widow, like the Jewish, was "the most destitute and wretched of all human beings." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Reformed (Ligonier):** Lamentations reflects that "even the prophet Jeremiah, who saw Babylon's conquering of Judah as entirely just, was amazed by the horrors." The fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. was God's ultimate covenant curse (Lev 26:14–39; Deut 28:15–68). — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lamentations-jeremiah

---

### v. 2: "She weeps aloud in the night, with tears upon her cheeks. Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her. All her friends have betrayed her; they have become her enemies."

*   **Gill:** "Weeping weeps" — two weepings, one for the first temple, one for the second (per Talmud). She weeps in the night because that is when the temple was burnt. The "lovers" are the idols she followed, now useless; or the nations (Assyrians, Egyptians) who were her allies. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Ellicott:** The sorrow is intensified because "the tears do not cease even in the time which commonly brings rest." "Lovers" and "friends" are Egypt (Jer 2:36), Edomites, Moabites and others with which Judah had alliances and which now turned against her (see Ps 137:7; Ezek 25:3–6). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Pulpit:** The national God was conceived as the Husband of the nation; the prophets retained and elevated this idea. The "lovers" phrase is a favourite of Jeremiah (Jer 3:1; 4:30; 22:20, 22; 30:14) but also of Hosea (2:5, 7, 10, 12, 13) and Ezekiel (16:33, 36, 37). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/1.htm

*   **Guzik (Enduring Word/Pentecostal-charismatic):** Jeremiah shows no triumph despite his prophecies being vindicated; "there is no exultation… there is a twofold loyalty manifest throughout, first to God in the confession of sin, and then to his people in the expression of their sorrow" (quoting G. Campbell Morgan). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 3: "Judah has gone into exile under affliction and harsh slavery; she dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest. All her pursuers have overtaken her in the midst of her distress."

*   **Ellicott:** The Hebrew could mean "from affliction" — forcible deportation from misery at home to worse misery in Babylon. They found no "rest" (Deut 28:65). Persecutors "hunted them down to the 'straits' from which no escape was possible." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** Two possible readings: (1) Judah went into captivity *because of* their sins in oppressing the poor and not freeing servants after seven years (Jer 34:13), or (2) "through affliction" — the affliction and servitude imposed by the Chaldeans. "Between the straits" is interpreted by a Midrash as the period between the 17th of Tammuz and the 9th of Ab — the three weeks of mourning in Jewish tradition. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Pulpit Commentary:** The poet is thinking of Jews who sought refuge in foreign lands (Jer 40:11), not only those deported. Keil retains the view that the Jews passed "out of" the misery of the invasions into the misery of captivity. "Between the straits" recalls Ps 118:5 — a narrow place symbolizing adversity, contrasted with "a large place" meaning prosperity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/1.htm

*   **Constable:** Judah was out of the Promised Land where God said she would find rest (Deut 12:10; 25:19; Josh 21:44). "Now there was no rest for her, but only distress, as the people lived among the Gentiles." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 4: "The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to her appointed feasts. All her gates are deserted; her priests groan, her maidens grieve, and she herself is bitter with anguish."

*   **Ellicott:** This paints the "religious desolation" of Jerusalem. The roads and gates were no longer thronged with pilgrims and worshippers. "Virgins" are joined with "priests" because they took part in the hymns and processions of the great festivals (Ex 15:20; Ps 68:25; Jdg 21:19–21; Jer 31:13). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** "The ways of Zion do mourn" is a rhetorical figure — roads appear joyful when crowded with travellers and mournful when empty. The "gates" are desolate both because no one goes in and out and because the elders no longer sit there for judgment. Priests sigh because the temple is burnt and sacrifices have ceased. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** Calls this "a fine prosopopoeia" — the roads themselves shed tears. He compares classical poets: Moschus (Epitaph on Bion) and Virgil (Eclogue V), who similarly personify nature mourning. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Precept Austin (Study Bible notes):** "The tragedy that had overtaken the nation had now overtaken the center of their religious life — Zion." The appointed festivals are gone and everything is deserted. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

---

### v. 5: "Her foes have become her masters; her enemies are at ease. For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions. Her children have gone away as captives before the enemy."

*   **Ellicott:** "Her adversaries are the chief" — literally "have become the head," fulfilling Deut 28:13 in reverse. "Her enemies prosper" — better, "are at ease, secure from every resistance on her part." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Precept Austin:** "Now for the first time the name of the Lord (Yahweh) is introduced as the One who had made Judah suffer because of her many transgressions." This is the theological heart of the lament. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

*   **Guzik (Enduring Word):** The word for "transgressions" (*pesha*) is "essentially a secular word meaning 'rebellion'" (quoting Ellison). Jeremiah understood this was not due to fate or blind history — "It was because Judah had sinned so long and so deep that it was God's will to afflict her." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Constable:** "Over and over again [Jeremiah] affirmed that the Lord Himself had decreed (Lam 1:17; 2:17; 3:37-38) and sent the calamity (Lam 1:5, 12-15; 2:1-8; 3:1, 43-45; 4:11)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** The Chaldeans were only instruments; "the evil was from the Lord, according to his will and righteous determination." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 6: "All the splendor has departed from the Daughter of Zion. Her princes are like deer that find no pasture; they lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter."

*   **Gill:** "All her beauty is departed" — the kingdom removed, the priesthood ceased, the temple burnt, palaces demolished. "Her princes are become like harts that find no pasture" — heartless, without courage, fearful. The Targum reads: "her princes run about for food, as harts run about in the wilderness." They "are gone without strength before the pursuer." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Precept Austin:** "Like stags running away from hunters, leaving no one to defend the herd, so Judah's leaders had abandoned the nation (2Ki 24:1, 12; Dan 1:2) — as did King Zedekiah when he fled for his life during the siege (2Ki 25:4)." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

*   **Guzik:** The image of "pastureless deer contrasts sharply with the situation depicted in Psalm 23" (quoting Harrison). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **JFB (from search excerpt):** Notes that Jarchi observes the word for "pursuer" has here all its letters (unusually full spelling in Hebrew), denoting the full pursuit and complete victory of the enemy. — (seen at biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/lamentations/1.htm)

---

### v. 7: "In the days of her affliction and wandering Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old. When her people fell into enemy hands she received no help. Her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall."

*   **Gill:** The "pleasant things" include civil and religious liberties, the temple, altars, the ark, the prophets, peace and prosperity. "None did help her" — not the Egyptians, her allies. Enemies "did mock at her sabbaths." Gill notes this could be read as "mocked at her cessations" — i.e., at the good things that ceased. The Romans mocked Jews as "Sabbatarians" for idleness. Juvenal satirized them for losing a seventh part of life. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** Defends the reading "Sabbaths." The Septuagint has "her habitation," the Chaldee "her good things," the Syriac "her breach." But Clarke notes many Hebrew MSS read the plural "her Sabbaths" and argues the heathen did mock Jewish Sabbath observance. Seneca complained the Jews "lost the seventh part of their life in keeping their Sabbaths." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** "The tragedy of Jerusalem's fall was worse after considering how things were once so much better. The memory of days of pleasant things stung in the days of her affliction and roaming." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 8: "Jerusalem has sinned greatly; therefore she has become an object of scorn. All who honored her now despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; she herself groans and turns away."

*   **Gill:** "Jerusalem hath grievously sinned" — literally "hath sinned a sin," a great sin (idolatry or covenant-breaking). "Therefore she is removed" — or "for separation," like a menstruous woman, defiled and separated from society. "They have seen her nakedness" — stripped of all good things, "both her weakness and her wickedness being exposed." She "sigheth and turneth backward" — covered with shame. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** "The once dignified city was humiliated and exposed. Like a queen stripped of her royal robes." Ellison says: "Here she is compared to a debased, slatternly harlot, shamelessly exposing her nakedness and indifferent to the marks of menstrual blood." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Constable:** Jerusalem's great sinning resulted in her becoming "unclean and despised, like an overexposed woman. She had embarrassed herself; her sins and vices had come to the light." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 9: "Her uncleanness stains her skirts; she did not consider her end. Her downfall was astounding; there was no one to comfort her. Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!"

*   **Gill:** "Her filthiness is in her skirts" — her sin is manifest in her punishment. The allusion is to a menstruous woman whose blood flows down to the skirts. "She remembereth not her last end" — she did not consider in prosperity what sin would bring. "Therefore she came down wonderfully" — literally "with wonders," astonishing all observers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** Jerusalem "never thought about where her path of sin and rebellion would lead her. Her lack of forethought meant her collapse was awesome." The first prayer breaks in: "O LORD, behold my affliction" — with no comforter, "all Jerusalem could do was cry out to the God she had rejected." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Constable:** The city fell because "it had not considered the consequences of its apostasy (cf. Deut 32:29; Isa 47:7). Sin had stuck to her like dirt to the hem of a garment (cf. Lev 5:3; 7:21)." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 10: "The adversary has seized all her treasures. For she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary — those You had forbidden to enter Your assembly."

*   **Ellicott:** "Pleasant things" primarily refers to the vessels of the Temple (2 Chr 36:10, 19), but the word has a wider range. Stress is laid on the *profanation* rather than the plunder. Ammonites and Moabites were excluded from the congregation in Deut 23:3, "and yet they and other heathen nations now rushed even into the Holy of Holies." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** Jarchi interprets the enemy as the Moabites and Ammonites who seized the books of the Law and burnt them, "because there was a law in them that forbid them entering into the congregation of Israel." But the Targum better explains it of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Precept Austin:** "Judah lost the most outstanding of all her glorious possessions — the temple of God. The sanctuary was off limits to Gentiles previously, but now the nations tramped through it with disregard." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

*   **Constable:** Jerusalem's enemy gained control because "she had not kept the temple holy. The Judahites had allowed pagan people to worship with them and so had diluted their allegiance to Yahweh." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 11: "All her people groan as they search for bread. They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive. Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised."

*   **Ellicott:** The famine sufferings are in the present tense — either vivid historic present or because sufferings still continued after the capture. The remnant "had to bring out their treasures, jewels, and the like, and offer them for bread." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** "They have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul" — literally "to cause the soul to return," to fetch it back when fainting through famine. They would part with rich clothes, jewels, anything, for food. The prayer "See, O Lord, and consider; for I am become vile" expresses her condition as "mean, base, and contemptible" through poverty and want. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** "Jerusalem is compared to a woman brought into great straits, who parts with her jewels and trinkets in order to purchase by them the necessaries of life." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 12: "Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see! Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?"

*   **Ellicott:** The Hebrew is literally "Not to you, ye passers by" — which the AV takes as a question. The LXX and Vulgate take it as an interjection: "O all ye that pass by…" "What the mourning city felt most keenly was that her unparalleled sufferings were met with an unparalleled indifference." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Preached an entire sermon on this verse ("Is It Nothing to You?"). He describes Jerusalem as "sitting by the wayside like a maiden who has been sore wounded … crying out in her loveliness and anguish." He says: "In all the annals of history there never was sorrow equal to the fate of Jerusalem. Many cities have been destroyed, but none have fallen amid such a tempest of terrors." He applies it to Christ's sorrows and to the need for Christian sympathy. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/is-it-nothing-to-you

*   **Clarke:** "The desolations and distress brought upon this city and its inhabitants had scarcely any parallel. Excessive abuse of God's accumulated mercies calls for singular and exemplary punishment." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** "Jerusalem felt what many sufferers feel; that her sorrow was incomparable to others and incomprehensible to others." Yet Jerusalem knew the true source: "It was not the Babylonians; it was the LORD who had inflicted this devastation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 13: "He sent fire from on high, and it overpowered my bones. He spread a net for my feet and turned me back. He made me desolate, faint all the day long."

*   **Ellicott:** "From above" — "The judgments that had fallen on Jerusalem were as a fire from heaven, piercing even to 'the joints and marrow.'" "He hath turned me back" — not defeat in battle but, completing the figure of the net, paints "the failure of every effort to escape." The word for "desolate" implies "an utter, hopeless misery" (as Tamar in 2 Sam 13:20). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Constable:** "The Lord had sent fire into the city's bones when he allowed the Babylonians to burn it. He had captured Jerusalem as a bird in His net." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Precept Austin:** Four metaphors depict God's judgment: fire from heaven (Gen 19:24; Ps 11:6), a hunter's net (Ps 94:13; Jer 50:24; Ezek 12:13), an animal yoke (Jer 28), and being trampled like grapes (Isa 63:1–4; Rev 14:18–20). "The fire from on high was nothing less than fire from God." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

*   **Guzik:** "Not Jerusalem's enemies, but God himself had entrapped the city, bringing it to an inescapable and ignominious end" (quoting Ellison). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 14: "My transgressions are bound into a yoke, knit together by His hand; they are draped over my neck, and the Lord has broken my strength. He has delivered me into the hands of those I cannot withstand."

*   **Ellicott:** The verb for "bound" is not found elsewhere — probably a technical term for twisting the thongs by which a yoke was fastened. The "yoke" is Judah's transgressions, "a sore burden too heavy to be borne." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** "I am now tied and bound by the chain of my sins; and it is so wreathed, so doubled and twisted round me, that I cannot free myself. A fine representation of the miseries of a penitent soul, which feels that nothing but the pitifulness of God's mercy can loose it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** Jeremiah pictures Jerusalem bound like a brute ox, "yet the yoke was fashioned out of their own transgressions. It was bound to them by cords woven by God's own hands." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 15: "The Lord has rejected all the mighty men in my midst; He has summoned an army against me to crush my young warriors. Like grapes in a winepress, the Lord has trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah."

*   **Ellicott:** "Trodden under foot" — better, "hath made contemptible." "Mighty men" — the adjective is used elsewhere of bulls (Ps 22:12; Isa 34:7) but stands here for the heroes of Judah who fell "not in open battle, but ignominiously 'in the midst' of the captured city." "He hath called an assembly" — the phrase is the one commonly used for proclaiming a religious festival (Lev 23:4); here the festival is proclaimed *against* Jerusalem. "The Lord hath trodden the winepress for the virgin" — for the winepress as symbol of judgment, see Isa 63:2; Rev 14:19; 19:15. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill (via Poole cited in Guzik):** "God had trodden upon the Jews as men use to stamp grapes in a wine-press, where they use to crush them to pieces to get out the juice, and then they throw the husks, that are good for nothing, upon the dunghills." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Constable:** "He had trodden Jerusalem down as a virgin in a winepress. He had squeezed all the life out of her." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 16: "For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears. For there is no one nearby to comfort me, no one to revive my soul. My children are destitute because the enemy has prevailed."

*   **Ellicott:** "The unparalleled misery finds vent in a flood of bitterest tears. We note the emphasis of iteration in 'mine eye, mine eye.'" On "relieve" (or "revive") see the note on v. 11. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** "Sometimes Jeremiah is described as the weeping prophet, and he would agree with the description. Lamentations was not written with a dry eye, but with overflowing eyes." The worst aspect "was not the catastrophe of itself. It was that in the catastrophe, they had little or no sense of God's comfort or help." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

---

### v. 17: "Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her. The LORD has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes. Jerusalem has become an unclean thing among them."

*   **Ellicott:** "Zion spreadeth forth her hands" — "the normal attitude of Eastern prayer, or, perhaps, of lamentation and despair." "That his adversaries" — better, "that those round about him should be his adversaries, the nearest neighbours being the bitterest foes." "Jerusalem is as…" — "as one polluted, or as an abomination." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** "Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman, to whom none dared to approach, either to help or comfort, because of the law, Leviticus 15:19-27." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** "Jerusalem felt no comfort from God, and received none from man. By God's design (the LORD has commanded) all her neighbors had become her adversaries." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Precept Austin:** Notes this is the fourth time in the chapter the mournful refrain appears: "there is no one to comfort her" (also vv. 2, 9, 16, 21). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

---

### v. 18: "The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against His command. Listen, all you people; look upon my suffering. My young men and maidens have gone into captivity."

*   **Ellicott:** "'The LORD is righteous' — an echo from Jeremiah 12:1; 2 Chronicles 12:6. Misery does its work, and issues in repentance. The suffering comes from the all-righteous Judge." It may be significant that "with this beginning of conversion the name 'Jehovah' reappears." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** Cites Wright: "Again there is the confession which admits that God is in the right. This is often a hard admission to make. One can feel the agony of heart that is wrung out even while the people make confession." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Ironside (Plymouth Brethren):** "In this first chapter the remnant of Judah confess the righteousness of the Lord in permitting their afflictions, though they are filled with sorrow as they behold the sad results. They acknowledge their own sinfulness and extol the holiness of God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/lamentations-1.html

*   **Gill:** "The Lord is righteous" — He "is righteous in all his ways; the Chaldeans were but instruments." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 19: "I called out to my lovers, but they have betrayed me. My priests and elders perished in the city while they searched for food to keep themselves alive."

*   **Ellicott:** "I called for my lovers" — better, "to my lovers." The "lovers," as in v. 2, are the former allies of Judah. "The pressure of the famine of the besieged city is emphasised by the fact that even these, the honoured guides of the people, had died of hunger." A conjectural addition, "and found not," is supplied in the LXX and Syriac; but "rhetorically there is more force in the aposiopesis, the suggestive silence, of the Hebrew." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** "I called for my lovers — my allies; the Egyptians and others." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 20: "See, O LORD, how distressed I am! I am churning within; my heart is pounding within me, for I have been most rebellious. Outside, the sword bereaves; inside, there is death."

*   **Ellicott:** "Deserted by men, the mourner appeals to Jehovah. 'Bowels' and 'heart' are used almost as synonymous for the deepest emotions of the soul." The word for "troubled" (elsewhere Ps 75:8, used of colour) "might, perhaps, be better rendered inflamed." "At home there is as death" — the "as" gives "the emphasis of the undefined. It is not death pure and simple… but the starvation, disease, exhaustion, which all were deadly, i.e. deathlike, in their working" (comparing Virgil, *Aeneid* ii.369: *plurima mortis imago*). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Clarke:** "Abroad the sword bereaveth — WAR is through the country; and at home death; the pestilence and famine rage in the city." He compares Virgil (*Aeneid* ii.366), Milton (*Paradise Lost* XI.489), and Jeremiah 9:21 for the same image. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

---

### v. 21: "People have heard my groaning, but there is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that You have caused it. May You bring the day You have announced, so that they may become like me."

*   **Ellicott:** (From the search excerpts, this verse is treated as part of the concluding prayer for justice against the enemies who rejoiced.) The Adversaries heard and rejoiced; the response is a call for God's predicted judgment to fall on them.

*   **Guzik:** "Knowing that, the prophet prayed that their appointed judgment would come soon (do to them as You have done to me)." He cites Poole: "We may lawfully pray for such evils to the implacable enemies of the church and people of God, as may restrain and weaken their hands… we are only obliged by it to wish well to their souls, and to desire no evil against them out of private revenge." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Ironside:** Describes this as "a cry for vengeance not consistent with Christian light and privilege." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/lamentations-1.html

*   **Constable:** Jerusalem's enemies "had rejoiced over it. The city wished that God's predicted judgment of these enemies would come soon and that they would become like Jerusalem." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/lamentations-1.html

### v. 22: "Let all their wickedness come before You, and deal with them as You have dealt with me because of all my transgressions. For my groans are many, and my heart is faint."

*   **Clarke:** "Thou wilt call their crimes also into remembrance; and thou wilt do unto them by siege, sword, famine, and captivity, what thou hast done to me." He adds: "Imprecations in the sacred writings are generally to be understood as declarative of the evils they indicate; or, that such evils will take place. No prophet of God ever wished desolation on those against whom he was directed to prophesy." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

*   **Guzik:** Cites Wright: "The last two verses are a tentative prayer that God will vindicate His righteousness among the other nations. If Judah has needed to experience judgement to lead her to repentance, then others need the experience of judgement also." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

*   **Ironside:** "So the prayer goes up that the time may be hastened when all their wretchedness shall come before Him and He will do as He has said." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/lamentations-1.html

## Tradition-Specific Observations

### Reformed / Presbyterian
**Ligonier** emphasizes God's sovereign justice: Lamentations shows "there can be a godly grief over the fate of a people even when that fate is deserved." Even God "does not delight in the destruction of the wicked (Ezek 18:21–23)." The book teaches that "rejoicing in justice and righteousness do not preclude mourning for those who suffer because of their sin." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lamentations-jeremiah

### Baptist
**Spurgeon** preached on v. 12, applying it both to Jerusalem's fall and typologically to Christ's sufferings: "Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?" He emphasizes the moral seriousness of indifference to suffering and judgment, and calls Christians to active sympathy. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/is-it-nothing-to-you

### Wesleyan / Methodist
**Clarke** consistently emphasizes the moral and practical lessons: the widow as "the most destitute and wretched of all human beings"; the imprecations in v. 22 are "declarative" not vindictive — "No prophet of God ever wished desolation." He highlights the "penitent soul" imagery in v. 14. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/lamentations-1.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
**Guzik (Enduring Word)** draws attention to the experiential dimension: the "felt absence of God's comfort" as the worst agony; "When we suffer the consequences of our own sin, we should follow Jerusalem's example of confessing God's righteousness while still crying out to him." God is "the only source of true comfort and vindication, even in our deepest anguish." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-1/

### Plymouth Brethren
**Ironside** offers a dispensational reading. He describes vv. 21–22 as "a cry for vengeance not consistent with Christian light and privilege" — implying a distinction between the Old Testament remnant's prayer and New Testament ethics. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/lamentations-1.html
